Note: Genesis presents Eve as Adam’s wife and corresponding partner; together they become the parents of the first human family.
Cain is presented in Genesis as the first son of Adam and Eve.
Abel is presented in Genesis as a son of Adam and Eve and the younger brother of Cain.
Genesis 5 places Enoch in the seventh generation from Adam through Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, and Jared.
Genesis 5 places Noah in the tenth generation from Adam when Adam and Noah are counted inclusively, through the line of Seth.
Cain is presented in Genesis as the first son born to Eve.
Abel is presented in Genesis as a son of Eve and the younger brother of Cain.
The collection explicitly praises temples of Inanna, including her sanctuaries at Uruk and Agade, placing her cult within the wider sacred geography of Sumer and Akkad.
Inanna is the poem’s central deity and Enheduanna’s patron: her overwhelming powers are praised and her intervention is sought to reverse the narrator’s expulsion and restore her position.
Gilgamesh explicitly places his trust in Inanna before rejecting the elders’ advice and choosing resistance to Agga of Kish.

Secondary Name: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
Note: Enmerkar is described as chosen by Inanna, while Uruk and Aratta compete for her favor and for the prestige attached to her sanctuaries.
The rivalry is framed as a contest over Inanna’s favor; the conclusion declares Enmerkar her chosen and beloved lord.
Lugalbanda carries Enmerkar’s message to Inanna; she receives him favorably and gives the counsel that enables the campaign against Aratta to continue.
Inanna is the protagonist: she descends through the seven gates, is killed in the underworld, is restored through Enki’s intervention, and must provide a substitute for her return.
Inanna is explicitly identified as Dumuzi’s divine spouse, and the poem places his pursuit within the substitution cycle generated by her return from the underworld.
As Ishtar, she offers marriage to Gilgamesh; after his rejection she obtains the Bull of Heaven from Anu, setting in motion the offense that contributes to Enkidu’s death sentence.
The surviving Sumerian flood text explicitly says that holy Inanna lamented for her people during the catastrophe.
Inanna first establishes her sanctuary and favor at Agade, but later abandons the city; she also joins the gods who pronounce its curse after Naram-Sin’s attack on the Ekur.
The late legend presents Ishtar as the deity who loves and favors Sargon, turning his improbable rise from abandoned child to king into a story of divine election.

Noah and Utnapishtim both survive a divinely sent flood in a sealed vessel, preserve life, release birds, and offer sacrifice afterward. Their connection lies in a shared flood-narrative tradition that links the biblical account with older Mesopotamian formulations.
Inanna is called a daughter or beloved child of An in some Sumerian traditions, although other genealogies make her the daughter of Nanna or Enki.
Enlil is commonly treated as a son of An in Sumerian divine genealogy, though Mesopotamian genealogies were not completely uniform.
Some traditions call Enki a son of An, while others emphasize Nammu as his mother and source; the genealogy varies by text and period.
An and Ki form the paired cosmic principles of heaven and earth in Sumerian thought. They are sometimes treated genealogically, but Ki is not consistently represented as An’s fixed consort.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad
Note: An appears among the high gods invoked in the Akkadian royal tradition, helping place Sargon’s kingship within a supra-local divine order.
An is repeatedly invoked as the celestial authority who establishes temples, decrees destinies, and situates local sanctuaries within the wider divine order.
The hymn calls Inanna beloved of An and presents her cosmic rank as authorized by his command, placing her power within the hierarchy of the senior gods.

Secondary Name: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
Note: An is invoked among the senior gods whose authority frames Enmerkar’s kingship and the ordering of the lands, while Inanna remains the decisive patron of the contest.
The poem explicitly describes Ereš, the city of Nisaba, as a primeval city whose destiny was decreed by An and Enlil.
The list begins with kingship descending from heaven, indirectly connecting political sovereignty with the celestial divine order represented by An.
Anu appears as Ishtar’s father and as a senior god in the divine assembly; he releases the Bull of Heaven after Ishtar’s demand.
Anu is one of the senior gods who cannot overcome Tiamat; his failure helps prepare the gods’ transfer of supreme command to Marduk.
Anu is named in the series title and belongs to the divine framework through which celestial phenomena are interpreted as signs affecting kings and states.
Anu appears among the great gods invoked by Neo-Assyrian kings, although Ashur occupies the central position in the empire’s royal theology.
In a widespread Sumerian cosmogonic genealogy, Enlil is born from or emerges through the union and separation of An and Ki; the relationship is not identical in every tradition.
Gilgamesh is the central ruler of Uruk, shown consulting civic assemblies, choosing resistance, defeating Agga, and then releasing his defeated rival.
The poem centers on Gilgamesh’s death, funeral, and posthumous status, denying him bodily immortality while granting him lasting authority among the dead.
Gilgamesh is the epic’s hero-king; friendship with Enkidu, grief, and the failed search for immortality lead him toward acceptance of human limits and civic legacy.
Enlil is explicitly invoked at the opening of the hymn and participates in establishing the temple of Kesh within the divinely ordered cosmos.
Enlil belongs to the divine assembly responsible for the flood decree, while Enki covertly enables Ziusudra’s survival.
Enlil grants Sargon kingship, later withholds favorable signs from Naram-Sin, and becomes the principal divine power offended by the attack on his Ekur temple.
The lament presents Ur’s destruction as part of a divine decree associated above all with Enlil; mourning cannot reverse the decision, but the poem ultimately petitions for restoration.
Enlil is one of the highest authorities behind the catastrophe that devastates Sumer and Ur, while the lament gives ritual form to the cities’ and deities’ grief.
Enlil is Ninurta’s father and the senior divine authority whose household at Nippur receives and celebrates the warrior god’s victorious return.
Enlil responds to humanity’s noise with plague, drought, famine, and finally flood, while Ea repeatedly frustrates total destruction and helps establish a new demographic settlement.
Enlil participates in the divine decisions that limit heroic violence and appears prominently in Utnapishtim’s flood account, where Ea rebukes the indiscriminate destruction.
Enlil belongs to the divine court that validates Assyria’s case against the Babylonian king, casting Tukulti-Ninurta’s victory as punishment for broken oaths.
The epic transfers Enlil-like sovereignty to Marduk; among Marduk’s culminating titles he is acclaimed as the Enlil of the gods, absorbing the older office of divine kingship.
Babylonian theology, especially Enūma Eliš, presents Marduk as the son of Ea and Damkina.
Enki preserves humanity by communicating the flood warning to Ziusudra indirectly, circumventing the secrecy imposed by the divine assembly.

Secondary Name: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
Note: A celebrated and difficult passage invokes Enki or Nudimmud in relation to human speech and the ordering of lands; whether it imagines confusion or future unification of language remains debated.
Enki alone devises a remedy for Inanna’s death, creating two beings who obtain her corpse and revive it with the food and water of life.
As Ea, he repeatedly warns Atrahasis through indirect speech, defeats Enlil’s attempts at extermination, and proposes the post-flood limits on human reproduction and lifespan.
In the flood narrative Ea warns Utnapishtim through the wall of his house and later rebukes Enlil for using indiscriminate destruction rather than proportionate punishment.
The grouped incantation tradition belongs to the wider exorcistic world in which Ea or Enki was regarded as a source of healing, purification, and anti-demonic knowledge.
Ea kills Apsu, establishes his dwelling upon the defeated abyss, fathers Marduk, and later helps Marduk create humanity from Kingu’s blood.
Šurpu belongs to the exorcistic tradition in which Ea supplies ritual wisdom and Marduk or Asalluhi applies it to identify and release the sufferer from hidden oath, curse, guilt, or impurity.
The hymn praises the mother goddess of Kesh under names including Nintur and Aruru, divine forms closely associated with the broader Ninhursag mother-goddess tradition.
The flood text presents the mother goddess Nintur lamenting humanity’s destruction, connecting the composition with the broader Ninhursag complex of birth, fertility, and divine motherhood.
Humanity is created through the mother-goddess figures Mami, Nintu, and Bēlet-ilī, who belong to the overlapping theological complex represented elsewhere by Ninhursag.
The composition closes by praising Nisaba as the lady who completed the great tablets, explicitly associating the transmission of wisdom with the goddess of writing.
The final temple hymn praises Nisaba at Ereš as the wise goddess of tablets, measurement, and ordered knowledge; the collection itself ends with praise to her.
Nisaba is repeatedly named as patron of Ereš, and the composition ends with the formal acclamation “Nisaba, be praised.”
Nisaba is explicitly included among the gods who turn against Agade and pronounce the city’s curse after the desecration of Enlil’s sanctuary.
The list names Kug-Bau or Kubaba, a woman tavern-keeper who “made firm the foundations of Kish,” as king for one hundred years and founder of a Kish dynasty.

The laws emerged within the Assyrian state centered on the city and cult of Ashur, connecting the collection institutionally with the divine order under which Assyrian society and kingship were organized.
Ashur is the supreme Assyrian divine authority behind Tukulti-Ninurta’s campaign, while the poem presents the Babylonian king’s defeat as the consequence of violated oaths and divine judgment.
Ashur is repeatedly invoked as the god who chooses the king, commands campaigns, grants victory, and authorizes the expansion and restoration of Assyrian order.

Many court letters invoke Ashur in blessings, oaths, ritual reports, and statements of royal duty, showing how his authority entered the empire’s routine administration as well as its public ideology.
Enheduanna identifies herself in the tradition as daughter of Sargon of Akkad and was installed as high priestess of Nanna at Ur.

Secondary Name: Royal Inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad
Note: The inscriptions are issued in Sargon’s name and commemorate his victories, offerings, building activity, and claim to rule beyond the limits of a single city-state.
The poem explicitly names Sargon in its opening and recalls Enlil’s grant of kingship to him, using the founder’s divinely favored rise as the background to Naram-Sin’s later disaster.
Sargon is the legend’s first-person hero: secretly born, exposed in a basket, rescued by a water drawer, favored by Ishtar, and raised to kingship.
The collection’s colophon names Enheduanna as the compiler of the tablets. The attribution is ancient and explicit, although modern scholars continue to debate the extent and form of her authorship.
The first-person narrator identifies herself as Enheduanna and turns her expulsion, prayer, and restoration into a hymn proclaiming Inanna’s power.
The prologue and epilogue present Hammurabi as the king called by the gods to establish justice; the rulings are framed as evidence of his wise and divinely authorized government.

Enūma Eliš presents Tiamat and Apsu as the mingled primordial saltwater and freshwater powers from whom the first generations of gods arise, forming the cosmic pair that precedes the ordered divine world.
Tiamat becomes the leader of the divine forces opposing the younger gods; Marduk defeats and divides her body to construct the ordered cosmos.
Apsu is the primordial freshwater deity who plans to destroy the younger gods because of their disturbance; Ea kills him and establishes a dwelling over the defeated abyss.

The prologue describes Anu and Enlil elevating Marduk and granting Babylon preeminence. Marduk therefore legitimates the sacred status of Babylon within the order that authorizes Hammurabi’s kingship and legal rule.
Marduk is the epic’s victorious champion: he defeats Tiamat, organizes the cosmos, helps create humanity, and receives supreme kingship and fifty names from the assembled gods.

Nabonidus acknowledges Marduk within the traditional Babylonian pantheon and royal order, even while the inscription gives unusual emphasis to the moon god Sin and to the king’s restoration of ancient cults.
Marduk, often under the exorcistic identity Asalluhi, is invoked as the divine specialist who applies Ea’s wisdom to loosen curses, oaths, and hidden ritual pollution.

Both works preserve Mesopotamian traditions in which a divine decision brings a flood and a favored human survives through warning and boat-building. They represent related formulations of an older flood tradition, with Atrahasis surviving in a somewhat earlier written form.

Tablet XI of the Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic adapts extensive flood material known from Atrahasis, reshaping it as Utnapishtim’s lesson to Gilgamesh about mortality and the exceptional nature of his survival.

The collections share royal prologues, conditional judgments, compensation-based provisions, and the presentation of justice as a divinely authorized responsibility of kingship, demonstrating continuity within the Sumerian legal tradition.

Hammurabi’s collection continues the Mesopotamian genre of royal law collections while expanding its range of cases, penalties, and social distinctions within a different Babylonian political setting.

Both collections use conditional legal formulations and regulate household, property, injury, sexuality, and status, while adapting shared Mesopotamian legal reasoning to distinct Babylonian and Assyrian social orders.

The collections demonstrate the long survival of casuistic legal reasoning in Mesopotamia, particularly in matters of property, household organization, status, and compensation, despite their different political and scribal settings.
Both use elevated architectural and cosmic imagery to present temples as divinely ordered centers linking particular cities with the wider sacred landscape.

Both works are anciently attributed to Enheduanna and join temple theology with the authority of Inanna and the Akkadian royal-priestly order, although they differ sharply in genre and personal voice.
Both works center Inanna’s immense and dangerous power: the hymn celebrates her political and cosmic authority, while the myth confronts that authority with the independent laws of the underworld.

The texts belong to the same Dumuzi-underworld tradition: the Descent makes Dumuzi the substitute required for Inanna’s return, while Dumuzi’s Dream dramatizes his foreknowledge, pursuit, attempted escapes, and capture.

Both interpret political catastrophe through divine abandonment and violated cosmic order. The Curse concentrates blame on Naram-Sin, whereas the Lament ritualizes communal grief and petitions for Ur’s future restoration.

The two city laments share imagery of divine departure, invasion, ruined temples, and ritual mourning. The Lament for Sumer and Ur widens the catastrophe from Ur to the devastation of the broader land.

The two poems belong to the same Lugalbanda cycle and the same campaign against Aratta. Their literary narrative runs from Lugalbanda in the Mountain Cave to Lugalbanda and the Anzu Bird, even though the visualization places the Anzu poem slightly earlier within their shared broad date range.

Both emerged from Babylonian celestial scholarship but organized knowledge differently: Enūma Anu Enlil interpreted unusual heavenly phenomena as omens, while MUL.APIN systematized stars, risings, seasons, calendars, and schematic astronomy.

Secondary Name: Šumma ālu (If a City is Situated on a Height)
Note: The two series apply the conditional logic of Mesopotamian divination to different fields: Enūma Anu Enlil interprets celestial and meteorological signs, while Šumma Ālu addresses terrestrial, domestic, animal, and behavioral anomalies.
Genesis presents Cain and Abel as brothers; Cain’s killing of Abel becomes the first fratricide in the biblical narrative.
Enlil and Enki can be treated as brothers in traditions that make both sons of An, but Mesopotamian divine genealogies vary and do not preserve one universal family tree.
